💡 Key Takeaways

  • Latham & Watkins is introducing a upcoming program to reward its associates, setting aside $1 million for those who lead or contribute to artificial intelligence initiatives for the law firm and its clients in 2027.
  • All associates are eligible for the awards, which will be allocated after a nomination and review process in the spring, according to Reuters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, latham & Watkins is introducing a upcoming program to reward its associates, setting aside $1 million for those who lead or contribute to artificial intelligence initiatives for the law firm and its clients in 2027. (Photo by J Studios/Getty Images).

Latham & Watkins is introducing a upcoming program to reward its associates, setting aside $1 million for those who lead or contribute to artificial intelligence initiatives for the law firm and its clients in 2027.

All associates are eligible for the awards, which will be allocated after a nomination and review process in the spring, according to Reuters. The firm has noted awards will be “based on the significance, impact and scalability of each contribution.”.

Other firms also have launched programs around AI in recent months.

In a recent development, ropes & Gray is now allowing its more than 1,000 associates and counsels to credit 100 hours of AI experimentation and training toward their required billable hours, Reuters previously reported. Last year, the firm revealed that its first-year associates could devote up to 20% of their billable hours to AI testing.

Meanwhile, Kirkland & Ellis reportedly has said it will devote $500 million of its revenue to a custom AI platform over the next several years.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
  • Sources indicate that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of.
  • Sources indicate that your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of new databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

Sources indicate that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

Sources indicate that your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

The work spans three strength areas:.

Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

According to recent reports, we expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

Platform reliability & operations.

Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for new platform capabilities and major changes.

Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

Tooling, ecosystem & architecture.

Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):.

It has been revealed that tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers). You reason about trade-offs rather than reaching for defaults.

Software engineering — write real production code (Go and/or a comparable systems language) and can build controllers, operators, and platform APIs — stepping back to the underlying problem and building the right solution when no off-the-shelf tool fits.

Operational / SRE practice — are fluent in SLOs, error budgets, and operational KPIs; have led incident response and blameless postmortems; and have driven down MTTD/MTTR for systems you operated.

According to recent reports, have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems and understand isolation as a spectrum — from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and resource quotas through to stronger primitives such as virtual clusters (e.g. vCluster) or VM-class runtimes.

Operate confidently on AWS (multiple accounts, IAM, VPC) and are comfortable with infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine) and Kubernetes.

Script and automate to eliminate toil rather than absorb it.

Communicate clearly with both infrastructure specialists and product engineers, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

Experience building and operating a multi-tenant Kubernetes platform that internal teams deploy onto.

Familiarity with policy engines (Kyverno, or OPA/Gatekeeper) and cost-attribution tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) for per-tenant chargeback/showback.

Experience with managed database platforms or Postgres.

Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling.

According to recent reports, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Industry observers note that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

In a recent development, once a year, the entire firm gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

Sources indicate that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas will lead an undergraduate seminar at the University of Texas at Austin on race, equality and political thought in February.
  • The one-credit-hour seminar, “CIV 166 Equality and the New Birth of Freedom,” will include two hours of lecture daily from Feb.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas answers questions during a visit to the University of Texas at Austin on April 15, 2026. (Photo by Eric Gay/The Associated Press).

Recent findings suggest that U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas will lead an undergraduate seminar at the University of Texas at Austin on race, equality and political thought in February.

The one-credit-hour seminar, “CIV 166 Equality and the New Birth of Freedom,” will include two hours of lecture daily from Feb. 1 to Feb. 5, 2027, for 17 students. Sixty-five applied.

Students will also meet with Justin Dyer, the dean of the University of Texas at Austin’s School of Civic Leadership, during the seminar, which follows American political thought from the nation’s founding through the Civil War to the present.

Readings include the writings and speeches of Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois, as well as civil rights leaders the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The course examines how questions of race and equality show up in recent Supreme Court decisions.

Thomas previously spoke to students and legal professionals at the University of Texas at Austin in April, making the case that the Supreme Court’s failures have stemmed from a lack of courage, not a lack of understanding, and he discussed Plessy v. Ferguson, a 1896 ruling that upheld government-enforced segregation.

Thomas, who joined the Supreme Court in 1991, is its longest-serving current member.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job.
  • Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that diversity is at the heart of who we are at Xapo Bank. We’re a fully distributed team of over 160 Xapiens that work remotely from 50+ countries around the world.

Our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job. We work hard, think globally, and inspire each other to learn and grow. We are committed to changing the way things are done.

Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!

Xapo's product suite has grown from a Bitcoin vault into a full member proposition: BTC and USD accounts that pay interest, a global card with Bitcoin cashback, Bitcoin-backed loans, a growing suite of BTC wealth and credit products, and access to stocks, ETFs, and stablecoins, all inside one regulated relationship.

Xapo is a bank, and a bank earns on the money its members choose to hold with it. Each of those products shipped well. What hasn't yet existed is a single owner of the economics of the customer relationship: one person accountable for winning the right members, growing what they hold with us, and keeping them, and for the balance-sheet products that make that possible.

Industry observers note that the Chief Customer Officer is a new role at the top of the house, reporting to the CEO. You will run the stream that grows what members hold with Xapo, and you will own the Customer P&L, retail and institutional. It brings growth, client coverage, product management, and product design under one leader who is judged on customer contribution, the assets attracted and kept, and the members who stay. This is a customer-focused role in the most commercial sense: what a member earns from us, not the feature we shipped, is the centre of every decision.

The measure of success is a Customer P&L that grows on what members hold and keep: LTV:CAC improving, approved-to-paid rising, churn falling, and customer contribution the business can blueprint against.

It has been revealed that this is a banking role, not a requirements-gathering role, a marketing role, or a role you can run from a dashboard. Products are priced on the balance sheet and judged on the money they attract and keep.

This part matters as much as the mandate. The known failure mode for this role, in any manufacturer, is a CCO with a polished customer-insight deck and no ownership of the number. That is disqualifying here.

Day 30: The Customer P&L baseline is documented across retail and institutional: customer contribution, LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, net paid-member growth, and assets attracted and kept. You have formed your own independent view of where members are won, lost, and under-served, and shared it with the CEO and Board.Day 60: The unified Customer operating model is live: one set of key results across Growth, Client Coverage, Mission PMs, and Product Design, read weekly from one source. Every mission PM owns a product's contribution and its price, and the roadmap is ranked on what it earns, built with Finance and the line leads.Day 90: At least one measurable improvement in LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, or net new AUM flow is live and attributable to a change you made, not a feature ship, an outcome moved. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, calling a judge a vulgar name is rude, but it does not amount to criminal contempt, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court recently found. (Image from Shutterstock).

The criminal contempt conviction of a courtroom spectator who called a judge a vulgar name after she ruled against a motion that his acquaintance filed was recently vacated by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.

Recent findings suggest that basile Outlaw spent 30 days in jail after the 2022 incident involving Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington, Reason reports.

“What did you say?” Covington responded to his remark, according to the article.

“Never mind, I’m leaving,” Outlaw said.

He claims that he later came back to apologize and was taken into custody, Reason reports.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2023, the Pennsylvania Superior Court upheld Outlaw’s conviction. The state supreme court reversed and vacated the conviction in late October, finding that while what Outlaw did was rude, it wasn’t enough for criminal contempt.

The majority opinion cited an earlier finding involving a pro se party in a custody dispute calling the judge a vulgar term.

According to recent reports, here, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court also reversed a criminal contempt conviction for the party. In both cases, the state supreme court found, the outbursts amounted to momentary breaks in the proceedings, not significant disruptions.

  • Reuters reported Wednesday that regulators alleged that Mildon steered a 21-year-old club employee, Alice Bianco, into a $15,000 settlement of misconduct claims against her boss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 12, 2026, 11:16 am CST.

It has been revealed that alina Habba Mildon at the White House in March 2025. (Photo by Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post).

According to recent reports, the New Jersey Office of Attorney Ethics filed a disciplinary complaint Tuesday against Alina Habba Mildon—a former personal lawyer to President Donald Trump and a former acting U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey—over her role in settling a 2021 sexual harassment dispute at the Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, where she was a paying member.

Reuters reported Wednesday that regulators alleged that Mildon steered a 21-year-old club employee, Alice Bianco, into a $15,000 settlement of misconduct claims against her boss.

Sources indicate that according to Reuters, Mildon allegedly persuaded Bianco to stop communicating with her attorney, potentially confusing Bianco into thinking that Mildon was acting as her lawyer. The complaint also alleged that Mildon undervalued the claims in a way that benefited the club and did not disclose her financial ties to it. Mildon became a personal lawyer to Trump soon afterward.

Bianco later hired attorney Nancy Smith, who sued the club in 2023 and settled for $400,000. In a statement to Reuters, Smith claimed that Mildon “got ​my client to terminate her lawyer, accept a ridiculously low settlement, ​and agree to an illegal nondisclosure agreement, silencing her.”.

Smith added that she thought that Mildon’s “numerous ethics violations in that scenario should result in disbarment.”.

Mildon’s attorney, Kim Ringler, told Reuters that “the complaint ⁠starts a long process for resolving concerns about conduct that took place more than five years ago.”.

The complaint adds to Mildon’s recent troubles. A federal judge ruled last year that her appointment as New Jersey’s top federal prosecutor was unlawful. Trump also publicly called a $50 million contract that she obtained while at the Department of Justice “unacceptable,” and the New York Times reported Tuesday that she has since lost it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 12, 2026, 12:12 pm CST.

    In a recent development, british comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London during his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The judge who sentenced British comedian and actor Russell Brand is being given high marks for his sentencing comments, particularly for clarifying rape myths that were presented during the trial.

    Industry observers note that high Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan sentenced Brand to 10-and-a-half years in prison Monday. In his comments, Bennathan addressed myths surrounding rape and the “enablers” who witnessed Brand’s sexual assaults on women.

    “The judge’s comments are welcome given the significant role that rape myths played in this trial, which in turn have influenced public discussions about the case,” mentioned Deniz Uğur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, according to coverage by the Guardian.

    Executives from the Criminal Bar Association of England and Wales noted the “piercing clarity of the judge’s statement.” The judge’s comments were also called “hugely important” because of how high-profile the trial was, according to Ciara Bergman, the CEO of Rape Crisis England & Wales.

    Bergman pointed out that Bennathan’s remarks starkly countered misconceptions presented by the defense attorney, Ian Winter, including that the women should have fought back, screamed or immediately reported the attack.

    “Of course, this is not the case; there are a range of ways in which people respond to the threat of an imminent sexual assault, and all of them are valid,” Bergman mentioned.

    A Fresh York attorney was sentenced Thursday to eight months in prison for embezzling over $500,000 from a trust that he oversaw. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A Latest York attorney was sentenced Thursday to eight months in prison for embezzling over $500,000 from a trust that he oversaw, according to the Connecticut U.S. attorney’s office.

    Edward W. Miller, 71, of Lawrence, Latest York, was sentenced to prison by U.S. District Judge Sarala V. Nagala in Hartford, Connecticut.

    Sources indicate that david X. Sullivan, the U.S. attorney for the District of Connecticut, confirmed the sentence after Miller was found guilty of stealing more than $500,000 from a property trust that he managed from February 2016 to September 2022, owned by a person identified as “M.P.” in court records.

    Miller used his position as a trustee to write and negotiate unauthorized checks that he then made payable to himself, his law practice and family members, according to prosecutors and coverage by Law360.

    Miller pleaded guilty to wire fraud earlier this year and noted he refinanced his home to pay back the trust. Miller made full restitution of $509,372.82, part of a settlement of a separate civil lawsuit filed by the victims.

    In addition to eight months in prison, Miller was also sentenced to one year of supervised release.

    Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher has snagged a large part of soon-to-be defunct Weil, Gotshal & Manges, including its co-managing partner.

    Reuters reported Thursday that Gibson Dunn has confirmed that it will bring aboard a 120-lawyer private funds group from Weil Gotshal, including co-managing partner Jonathon Soler.

    According to Reuters, the group will include 23 partners across Latest York; Washington, D.C.; and London and is set to start at Gibson Dunn in January.

    “This is the most sought-after ​cross-border funds team in the market, and their arrival is a ⁠defining moment for our practice,” said Shukie Grossman, the global chair of Gibson Dunn’s investment funds ​practice, in a statement.

    The hires land days after Weil Gotshal’s partners voted earlier this week to wind down the 95-year-old law firm, a decision that followed an Oct. 28 recommendation from leadership.

    According to Reuters, several firms have started, or are the in process of, absorbing groups of lawyers from the closing firm. Kirkland & Ellis stated last week 40 lawyers will join, including private equity partner Ramona Nee, who had been in line to lead Weil Gotshal and was a co-managing partner alongside Soler.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom said Thursday it has hired three Weil Gotshal partners, adding to the two it picked up before the dissolution. Kirkland; Latham & Watkins; Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison; Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson; and Massumi + Consoli have also announced or confirmed Weil Gotshal partner hires this week.

    Soler did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

    Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure.

    • An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 16, 2026, 12:52 pm CST.

    According to recent reports, an Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock).

    An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

    It has been revealed that anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

    Recent findings suggest that court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

    The officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

    According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”.

    Fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

    LexLab, the legal technology hub at the University of California College of the Law at San Francisco, is launching a three-day artificial intelligence legal tool building course, Law & AI Certificate Lab.

    The intensive LAIC Lab course, offered Dec. 1-3, is a condensed, intensive version of one offered to law students over the course of a semester, offering lawyers and leaders a deep dive into the logic underlying legal AI while offering hands-on exploration of AI systems.

    The course allows students to work with AI company Legora and AI platform Harvey as well as Replit, an app and website builder.

    At the end of the certificate program, students should be able to move beyond using “chat” to build repeatable playbooks, checklists and other workflows; evaluate AI tools and vendors; determine whether tech should be bought or built; and manage privilege, confidentiality, conflicts and competence issues in AI-augmented practice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court Building is closed today for Veterans Day. In recognition of that, this is an abridged edition of SCOTUStoday.

    Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration has brought the battle over construction of a fresh White House ballroom back to the Supreme Court. In a petition for review filed last week but made public on Monday, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.” For more on the petition, see the On Site section below.

    On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

    On Friday, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at a Boston airport in 2025. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at the Boston Logan International Airport in September 2025.

    Industry observers note that U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the District of Massachusetts also found that federal agents likely violated the First Amendment rights of Andrew Lattarulo, a co-owner of the law firm Georges Cote in Massachusetts. Lattarulo runs an Instagram account featuring videos explaining immigrants’ rights and critiquing federal immigration policies.

    After agents seized Lattarulo’s phone without a warrant and downloaded a copy of its contents, they returned the phone. The government has claimed that the seizure was part of an investigation into his firm for potentially employing unauthorized immigrants.

    Lattarulo’s lawsuit alleges that agents targeted him because of his advocacy and seized information that included confidential communications with his clients.

    Burroughs’ ruling mandates that federal officials preserve all copied cellphone data without accessing it as litigation continues, according to a story by Law.com.

    #43899. Eleven new relists in search of four votes

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4582 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Eleven new relists in search of four votes

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference.
    • The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser.
    • After a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 new relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

    First, some old business. The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser. After three relists, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown finally got the nod. The court will decide when bankruptcy courts can refuse to enforce arbitration agreements in suits alleging violations of the automatic stay. But two-time relist Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia struck out: The court denied without comment the petition brought by Roberto Clemente’s family over Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image, which raised questions about takings of intangible property and Puerto Rico’s sovereign immunity.

    After a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 new relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week. Several come in pairs or trios, and the federal government – the court’s most successful repeat litigant – advocates review in three of them.

    Recent findings suggest that the government seeks asylum – from the D.C. Circuit.

    The most consequential new relist this week may be Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. On his first day back in office, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10888, which suspended the entry of aliens “engaged in the invasion across the southern border” and barred those who violate the suspension from invoking provisions of the immigration laws that would let them stay, including asylum.

    It has been revealed that three nonprofits and 13 individuals sued. The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States. It held unlawful the proclamation’s restrictions on asylum and other statutory protections, as well as its authorization of removal procedures outside those established by Congress, and issued a classwide injunction. A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit narrowed the class definition, but affirmed. It reasoned that although asylum is discretionary, the executive cannot categorically deny covered migrants access to asylum by proclamation and informal guidance rather than through the procedures Congress prescribed. Judge Justin Walker dissented in relevant part.

    The solicitor general’s petition argues that asylum is discretionary and that the president may categorically deny it to those covered by the proclamation. Requiring the government to accept applications it has already decided to reject, the government contends, serves no purpose. It also challenges the classwide injunction and the breadth of the certified class. The government argues that the ruling threatens to revive chaos at the border. Iowa and 21 other states support the petition, arguing that the decision undermines the federal duty to protect the states against invasion.

    Industry observers note that the respondents’ brief in opposition argues that Congress expressly gave noncitizens physically present in the United States the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered, and that the president cannot eliminate that right by proclamation. They emphasize the absence of a circuit split and dispute the government’s claims that the policy was responsible for reducing border crossings. They call the remedial challenges fact-bound and say the government overstates the border crisis, noting that apprehensions had already fallen more than 90% from their peak before the proclamation.

    It has been revealed that the D.C. Circuit’s mandate is stayed, leaving the asylum restrictions in place for now. The absence of a split weighs against review, but the invalidation of a major administration policy could well persuade the justices to take another trip to the border. Will the court resolve this case rapidly or let it sit for a while as it decides what to do, as it has in other high-profile cases?

    Our first group of cases asks whether Washington may regulate private companies that run federal immigration detention centers. In GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, a class of detainees and the state sued GEO, which operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma under a federal contract, for not paying Washington’s minimum wage to detainees in a voluntary work program for which ICE reimburses $1 a day. GEO argues it’s not a conventional labor relationship, but just an effort to prevent the detainees from becoming restless from idleness. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit certified the question to the Washington Supreme Court, which held that the state minimum-wage law applied to the detained workers. A divided panel of the 9th Circuit then rejected GEO’s supremacy clause defenses, leaving GEO with a judgment it puts at about $37 million. Seven judges voted to rehear the case en banc, and six joined dissents, arguing that (among other things) the state law “interferes with federal immigration-detention policy” and thus directly regulates the federal government.

    Industry observers note that GEO argues that Washington cannot regulate a federal detention program through a contractor while exempting its own detainees from the wage law. Washington and the detainees respond that the law applies equally to every private detention contractor, whether it works for a city, the state or the federal government, and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit applies the same test as the 9th. The detainees also note that ICE has since revised its detention standards, which they say limits the decision’s future impact.

    In a recent development, in a court-invited amicus brief, the U.S. solicitor general recommends granting review. The government argues that the law discriminates against the federal government, because Washington exempts its own facilities while barring itself from contracting with private ones, and that federal statutes leave detainee pay to the Secretary of Homeland Security. It also indicates the decision conflicts with a decision of the 3rd Circuit ruling on a Latest Jersey law targeting private detention contractors.

    According to recent reports, GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson challenges a 2023 Washington statute regulating private civil detention facilities, which GEO says reaches its Tacoma facility alone. The district court preliminarily enjoined it, but the 9th Circuit vacated that ruling, rejecting GEO’s direct regulation and preemption claims and remanding on its discrimination claim against private contractors. GEO says Washington is micromanaging federal detention by regulating a contractor; the state says its requirements resemble those governing other civil facilities. It also points to further proceedings on remand as a reason not to intervene yet.

    A grant in Nwauzor seems likely; Ferguson presents a closer question, but at minimum it seems likely to be held if Nwauzor is granted.

    Two companies that went public while business was booming present a question of required disclosures in federal securities filings: How much bad news must a company reveal? Two related relists ask the justices to clarify when withholding information makes an IPO registration statement misleading under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933.

    Recent findings suggest that in Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, the online brokerage rode the GameStop meme-stock frenzy and Dogecoin boom into its July 2021 IPO. Robinhood warned that trading might decline and provided an estimate of second-quarter revenue, but investors say it withheld information showing that trading and other business metrics were already declining. A district court dismissed their claims, but a divided panel of the 9th Circuit revived them. Robinhood’s petition argues that merely omitting material information cannot create liability unless the omission makes an affirmative statement misleading or violates a specific disclosure requirement. The investors respond that the organization’s disclosures presented a misleading picture of its performance. The U.S. solicitor general, invited to weigh in, recommends granting review on the Section 11 misleading-omissions question, but not on a separate question concerning disclosures of known trends under Item 303 of Regulation S-K (which the agency is reviewing).

    In ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, a webinar-platform provider prospered as businesses moved online during the pandemic. Investors allege that the manufacturer knew before the IPO that many pandemic-era customers did not intend to renew. An unpublished 9th Circuit memorandum revived the suit. ON24 asks whether describing an unmaterialized risk as hypothetical is misleading, alleging a split with the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd and 10th Circuits, and raises two questions that overlap with Robinhood’s. ON24 argues that the court improperly required it to predict future customer cancellations; the investors respond that “the warned-of risk was already materializing.” ON24 also asks the justices either to grant its petition or hold it for Robinhood. Leadersel Innotech answers that the 9th Circuit decision is non-precedential and that the panel found the risk had already begun to materialize.

    With the solicitor general supporting review in Robinhood, a grant there looks plausible. Whether ON24 gets invited along is less certain. It seems a likelier hold.

    It’s not every week that the Taliban is a respondent in the Supreme Court. That noted, it has not responded, leaving an Afghan diplomat filing an amicus brief to oppose review – not on the Taliban’s behalf, but on behalf of the Afghan people.

    When the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, the Treasury Department blocked billions of dollars that Da Afghanistan Bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Victims holding judgments against the Taliban sought to execute on the funds under Section 201(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which makes the blocked assets of a terrorist party and its “agency or instrumentality” subject to execution.

    A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover. It held that an entity’s status as a terrorist organization’s instrumentality must be determined when its assets were blocked, before the Taliban installed its officials at the bank. Separately, the panel rejected other plaintiffs’ attempt at prejudgment attachment, holding that Da Afghanistan Bank enjoys sovereign immunity as the central bank of Afghanistan, which the executive continues to recognize as a foreign state. Judge Richard Sullivan dissented.

    In Havlish v. The Taliban, judgment holders challenge the blocking-date rule, alleging a conflict between the 2nd Circuit and the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 9th and 11th Circuits. They are backed by Iowa and 30 other states.

    In a recent development, in Owens v. The Taliban, plaintiffs who lacked judgments when the district court ruled say the 2nd Circuit is the first court of appeals to require courts to defer to the executive on “foreign state” status, and thus “breaks with th[e] consensus” positions of the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd, and 6th Circuits. Ashton v. The Taliban joins Owens in arguing that courts should not defer to the executive branch in determining whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, and seeks a GVR in light of this year’s decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A.

    As noted, no respondent has appeared. The only opposition is an amicus brief jointly filed in the three cases by Naseer Faiq, chargé d’affaires of Afghanistan’s mission to the United Nations, who says no one is currently authorized to appear for Afghanistan in U.S. courts. He argues that the facts are unlikely to recur, that there is no circuit split, and that the immunity matter affects only the petitioners’ priority among creditors. The Havlish petitioners have sought leave to respond, arguing that the legal question is likely to recur in terrorism litigation and does indeed implicate a circuit split.

    At the very least, the court will need more time to figure out what to do when the respondent seems unwilling to appear to defend the cases.

    How many places can a state declare off-limits to firearms before the Second Amendment right to carry in public becomes largely theoretical? That’s the question in Novotny v. Moore, a challenge to Maryland’s extensive restrictions on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”.

    Industry observers note that maryland prohibits licensed gun owners from carrying firearms in numerous locations, including public transportation, parks and forests, healthcare facilities, museums, stadiums, casinos, public demonstrations, and establishments serving alcohol. I thought this was America! A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld those restrictions, finding historical support for them under the Supreme Court’s decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Judge G. Steven Agee dissented as to many of the restrictions, warning that the majority had stretched the sensitive-places exception too far. The panel separately struck down Maryland’s presumptive ban on carrying firearms on private property open to the public.(After this year’s decision in Wolford v. Lopez, which struck down Hawaii’s similar private-property rule, Maryland dropped its own cert petition seeking review of that ruling.).

    According to recent reports, the gun owners’ petition argues that historical restrictions on carrying firearms in sensitive places were generally limited to locations where the government provides security, not ordinary places where people gather. Maryland responds that historical regulations support restrictions at crowded places and locations serving vulnerable populations, and contends that review is unnecessary because the lower courts largely agree on the governing principles.

    Sources indicate that invoking Wolford, the petitioners ask the justices to grant review or at least send the case back for reconsideration. Whether the court is ready to take on the sensitive-places doctrine so soon after Wolford remains to be seen. But reconsideration under Wolford seems like a real possibility.

    In Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, the Commission fined Sprint $12.2 million and T-Mobile $80.1 million for failing to adequately safeguard customers’ location information shared with third-party aggregators, including by continuing to disclose the information after learning of significant security vulnerabilities. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the penalties, concluding that information about a cellphone’s location – even when no call is underway – qualifies as confidential “customer proprietary network information” under the Communications Act.

    It has been revealed that the carriers’ petition argues that the statute protects only call-location information, not all device-location data. They also contend that the FCC circumvented a statutory penalty cap by treating separate relationships with third-party companies as multiple “continuing violations,” and that the D.C. Circuit improperly deferred to the agency’s interpretation despite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. But the carriers’ principal request is narrower: They ask the justices to send the case back in light of this year’s decision in FCC v. AT&T, which held that an FCC forfeiture order does not itself compel payment. That opinion, the carriers say, rested on a key government concession: A firm can refuse to pay and contest the penalty in a subsequent enforcement proceeding with a jury. Sprint and T-Mobile say they paid under protest because the FCC’s orders demanded payment and existing precedent left them little choice. The government responds that the carriers always had the option not to pay, that they failed to preserve their claim of being misled, and that AT&T provides no reason for reconsideration. The carriers disagree.

    According to recent reports, A remand remains possible, although the government notes that the court rejected a comparable request from Verizon. For now, Sprint and T-Mobile are hoping the justices will take their call.

    How long can a “hot pursuit” stay hot after police lose sight of the suspect? That’s the question in City of North Las Vegas v. Jones, a case arising from a search for a suspected domestic abuser that ended with police entering a stranger’s backyard and shooting two dogs. The suspect was never found.

    Recent findings suggest that after officers saw a man flee over a backyard wall, the officers stated that they established a neighborhood perimeter rather than pursuing him on foot. A K-9 officer arrived about 18 minutes later, and during the ensuing search, his police dog alerted them toward a walled backyard. An officer climbed in without a warrant. Three pit bulls emerged, two of which attacked the police dog and were shot. The dogs’ owners, Genoa Jones and Cornell Tinsley, sued. The district court granted the officers qualified immunity, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed on the warrantless-entry claim, holding that the officers had not been in immediate and continuous pursuit and that circuit precedent clearly established the search’s illegality. It left intact qualified immunity for shooting the dogs. Eight judges dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc.

    Recent findings suggest that the city’s petition argues that the officers never abandoned the pursuit: They say they established a perimeter and used a police dog to locate a potentially dangerous suspect. Even if the search was unlawful, the city argues, no sufficiently specific precedent clearly established that fact. It also asks the justices to hold that only Supreme Court decisions – not lower-court precedent – can clearly establish law for qualified-immunity purposes. The homeowners respond that the officers never actually established a perimeter or chased the suspect and instead just conducted a neighborhood-wide search without knowing his whereabouts.

    It has been revealed that the eight dissenting judges may help keep the petition warm. But the court closely reviews many petitions in cases where police are denied qualified immunity, and unless the error was clear enough to warrant summary reversal, the justices may let this pursuit go cold – perhaps with a dissent from denial of cert.

    Sources indicate that the court has enough to chew on that it seems likely to take a while to finish processing this week’s latest offerings. As for me, I’ll be watching Monday’s orders to find out how much of this I get to reuse.

    #43894. Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1217 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v.
    • Recent findings suggest that the constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article II of the Constitution).
    • In a recent development, this case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards showed a court open to the possibility of a major limitation on the ability of agencies to impose fines or penalties under internal adjudicative processes, at least without ready review in court.

    Recent findings suggest that the constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article II of the Constitution). The Supreme Court always has recognized that it is permissible for officials in the executive branch – who don’t have the protections (including life tenure) that Article III gives to federal judges – to resolve questions in a proceeding that looks an awful lot like the kind of trial you might see in a federal court. And it also on several occasions has invalidated schemes that seemed to the court to go too far in that direction. To pick the most famous example, the justices invalidated the initial version of the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 because it gave undue adjudicative responsibility to bankruptcy “judges” that are not protected by Article III. What the court has never done well is explain exactly how far such powers can go. Nevertheless, recent decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a great willingness to rein in the powers traditionally granted to the administrative state.

    In a recent development, this case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States. Conventionally, when the Department of Labor decided that an employer had failed to treat workers as it promised pre-admission, it imposed fines or penalties in an administrative proceeding, often handing the funds over to the employees as compensation in the nature of back pay. The question for the justices is whether Article III of the Constitution can tolerate that dispute being resolved internally by DOL employees rather than by judges in a federal court.

    The government sees the dispute as squarely involving two categories of so-called “public rights” for which Article I treatment is permitted: the immigration power and public benefits. The immigration power is involved because the workers were permitted to enter the country on the condition that the employer treat them as agreed; the public benefit power is involved because the right to enter is a benefit almost entirely within the discretion of the executive.

    Several of the justices found that argument rather weak. Chief Justice John Roberts, for example, commented early on that the leading case about the immigration power (Oceanic Steam Navigation v Mellor) “had to do very much with entry, a condition of entry, and loathsome diseases. This strikes me as significantly different. … You’re trying to leverage an entry several weeks, months … in the past to the particular condition of work that doesn’t seem to have much to do with the actual entry.” For the chief justice, the government was trying to “leverage what is a significant barrier to entry, where you have a lot of deference to the executive branch,” and “trying to … extend that broad authority beyond the justification for its application.” He repeatedly emphasized that the specifics of the case “look more like a condition of employment rather than … entry.”.

    In a similar vein, Justice Amy Coney Barrett stated to Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris (arguing for the government): “I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our immigration tradition without an Article III court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different. …. So I’m … wondering here why that wouldn’t be the case for the alien. If the alien violated some sort of condition on the H-2A visa, why wouldn’t the alien be entitled to an Article III court before the alien had to pay that kind of a fine?” At which point Justice Neil Gorsuch chimed in that he “thought [an earlier case had remarked that] confiscating property goes to an Article III court when you’re trying to confiscate property from aliens. … I thought we decided a long time ago that you’ve got to go to an Article III court. Are … you resisting that?”.

    Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed to yet another precedent on civil penalties: “In Tull [v. United States], we mentioned … and this is 40 years ago – a civil penalty was a type of remedy at common law that could only be enforced in courts of law. …. That’s a fairly definitive statement in our precedent. What … are we supposed to do with that?”.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say that all of the justices sided against the government. Justice Elena Kagan, for example, found the case well within the boundaries of existing doctrine. To Harris, she commented early on: “[I]sn’t there a condition of entry here? … [T]hey wouldn’t be admitted unless the employer had promised certain things.” To Robert Johnson arguing on behalf of the employer – a different Robert Johnson, not the blues singer – she was much more pointed:.

    Offering a parallel perspective, Ketanji Brown Jackson emphasized that the court in numerous contexts has approved administrative adjudication of civil penalties. She repeatedly challenged Johnson to reconcile his argument with those decisions.

    It has been revealed that but ominous for the government was some repeated questioning of Harris about “the best way for you to lose” (as Justice Sonia Sotomayor put it). From early on in the argument, even the justices who seem most likely to accept the constitutionality of the arrangement were trying to help Harris identify the least damaging way for the court to rule against her. At the beginning of her argument and throughout it, Harris emphasized to the justices that a broad ruling against her on the constitutional question would unsettle programs in a wide variety of areas, ranging from Medicare, to government contracts, to student loans, but that did not seem to make any headway for her.

    According to recent reports, it is not at all clear from the argument how exactly the justices are going to come down. Clearly a significant group are considering the idea that an award of civil penalties is too far removed from the entry of the employee to be protected by the “public rights” doctrine that would protect administrative determination of the right to enter. My guess is that even those justices don’t yet know how far they would be willing to go – or how far they can go and secure five votes of agreement. I expect this case to come down late and be sharply divided.

    Correction (Nov. 15 at 6:12 p.m.): An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that “the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch” is in “Article I of the Constitution.”.

    Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

    • A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.
    • Federal prosecutors in New York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 17, 2026, 10:03 am CST.

    It has been revealed that A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.

    Federal prosecutors in New York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.

    According to Law360, a one-page form order signed Thursday by U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcia M. Henry of the Eastern District of Fresh York reveals that federal prosecutors and Balli are engaged in plea discussions.

    The order also shows that Balli’s defense counsel requested more time to focus on negotiations without the risk of not being adequately prepared for a trial, Law360 reports.

    Law360 requested but did not receive comment from either party.

    Balli began working for Cravath in 1989. According to prosecutors, he supported attorneys by producing legal documents and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings and at times had access to confidential information.

    Balli was arrested Thursday after prosecutors filed a criminal complaint against him and alleged that he made more than $70,000 in illicit profits.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    We believe that every human learns differently, and that technology can do more than entertain or save time.It can translate insight into transformation, through AI personalization, lean experimentation, and deep psychological understanding.

    Because learning shouldn’t just make you feel inspired for a day, it should change how you live, think, and create.

    At Paradox, we want to re-invent how people grow.

    We do not build another course or coaching app but the Operating System for Greatness.

    Founded by David Laroche - a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson, and Gad Elmaleh, Paradox aims to build something that will live beyond any individual (including its founder), for decades to come.

    Our ambition is to compete with players like Mindvalley (150M ARR), but with a sharper vision, grounded protocols for achievers, people who want more for their life, refusing mediocrity.

    To do that, we bring together designers, tech, coaches, and filmmakers to create learning experiences that are cinematic, precise, and effective.

    We move fast, aim high, and hold ourselves to the standards of Apple, Spotify, and MasterClass. No fluff, focused on meaningful impact.

    While others hide their numbers, we want to let our results speak loudly for us.

    Get obsessed with transforming our clients’ lives and let those transformations be our marketing.

    We want to build an AI-native firm, with agents in every department doing the work alongside our people.

    In product, that means building a self-learning AI for product management: a system that learns from every user signal, experiment and release, and gets sharper at deciding what to build next.

    For our clients, it means a self-learning AI that serves them through psychology and coaching, and gets better at helping each person change with every interaction.

    You won’t just use AI tools: you’ll help design the agents, loops and feedback systems that make Paradox learn faster than anyone else.

    -----------------------------------------.

    As Product Manager, you’ll be the architect of a new category, transforming growth into a living ecosystem powered by AI, behavioral science, and design.

    You won’t just build features, you’ll craft experiences that rewire behavior.

    You’re the architect bringing clarity between vision and execution, the person who turns “we should build this” into “it’s live, here’s the data and tangible impact.”.

    Every product cycle you lead will integrate:.

    Protocols : guided frameworks grounded in psychology that rewire perception, emotion, and action.

    Pods : human connection, accountability, and shared rituals.

    Loops : adaptive, AI-powered coaching cycles that evolve with each user.

    Personalization : experiences that feel uniquely theirs, every time.

    Recent findings suggest that going from a successful personal brand, to an international tech-driven iconic brand, is far from easy. It will be messy, chaotic - requiring constant iterations on MVPs and innovation in tech. Therefore to achieve this here are :.

    -----------------------------------------.

    Translate the founder’s strategic vision into a clear product strategy.

    Build and maintain the roadmap that connects business goals, user outcomes, and technological innovation.

    Ensure every feature supports the evolution of the Paradox ecosystem: Loops, PX Agents, Protocols, Membership.

    Be obsessed with user problems : talk to consumers weekly, analyze patterns, and identify where transformation breaks.

    Turn insights from behavioral science, coaching psychology, and learning design into actionable product hypotheses.

    Design loops, feedback, and rituals that make growth tangible.

    build for both the heart (inspiration) and the brain (structure).

    Apply Lean Startup methodology and scientific thinking to validate ideas through MVPs, not opinions.

    Design experiments and measurable success metrics before building.

    Iterate on a weekly basis on fresh hypothesis.

    Define and track product success metrics (activation, retention, transformation rates).

    Connect data to business KPIs, know how your product drives lifetime value, not just engagement.

    We don’t track metrics just for internal dashboards, we track them also to prove transformation.

    Help marketing leverage this data to fuel authentic, evidence-based storytelling — showing the world what real transformation looks like.

    Create a visceral experience that translates into emotions of inspiration, awe from users.

    Use a Science-backed, Cinematic, Contrarian style : Every product touchpoint should be grounded in behavioral science, expressed with cinematic beauty, and challenge conventions.

    -----------------------------------------.

    3–6 years as a Product Manager / Product Owner in EdTech, SaaS, or Consumer Tech.

    Bonus: experience in AI-driven products, learning design, or personal development platforms.

    You’ve shipped at least one major feature or product end-to-end, and can show measurable results.

    Uses Figma comfortably, prototypes directly.

    Craft-obsessed : You get things done, you love to work much beyond 9-5, you have a doer mentality, a bias for outcomes and want to be a beast in your field.

    User & Impact Obsessed: You think in outcomes, not outputs, you care about transformation.

    Analytical & System Thinker: You can turn a vague problem into a clear hypothesis, metrics, and roadmap.

    Digital & AI savvy : you’re able to build AI Agents (if not, you demonstrate ability to learn while applying).

    Cross-disciplinary Curiosity: You speak both tech and human; You can move from vision to spreadsheet to Figma.

    English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

    Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    --------------------------------.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos — wrong place.❌ If you prefer balance over intensity — wrong season.❌ If you build to deliver, not to elevate — wrong mission.

    ✅ If you’re obsessed with systems, psychology, and design…✅ If you dream of using AI to amplify what makes us human….

    Work with filmmakers, psychologists, engineers, and creatives obsessed with impact.

    -> 🏅Being surrounded by A-players who strive to perform.

    But you don’t just want a competitive paycheck, you also want….

    -> Playing a crucial role in the development of a company whose content and products will be used by millions of people.

    -> Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something!We receive messages every day from clients who have successfully lost weight, quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships, and made positive changes in their lives.

    -> ❤️ Contributing to the Paradox Foundation (our non-profit), dedicated to empower teenagers.

    But that's not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

    -> 😎A tech giant culture based on autonomy & accountability.

    -> 🌎A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

    -> 🏤Magnificent office in Dubai, Paris, Lisbon - it feels like home :).

    -> 🧍‍♀️Standing desks paid by the company if you live far from our offices.

    -> 📚150€ of books or education - At Paradox, we are learner lovers and we want to support you in that.

    -> 🔥6 1:1coachings - A Paradox Coach supporting you on anything personal or professional, we want you to live your best life.

    Here is your tailor made hiring process.

    📃 A 6 to 8 minutes application survey (with a short video assignment).

    💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

    💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, to discuss Product Vision and the next milestones to build.

    💼 Reference check to understand how you operate across environments and help set you up for a smooth onboarding.

    Our recruitment process is tailored to do our best to avoid that you or us realize that we’re not a perfect fit. Every step serves a purpose and will allow us to get to know you better as much as it’ll help you understand more where you’ll be stepping in.

    We also want you to have time to ask all of your questions regarding the mission, the long-term vision of your team and the organization, our values, with the relevant interlocutor in front of you.

    Let’s build the Operating System for Greatness.

    Industry observers note that during the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats on two of his signature initiatives – his efforts to limit birthright citizenship and impose sweeping tariffs – as well as his initial attempt to fire Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those challenges. In the wake of the court’s decisions in each of the three cases, Trump continues to fight on, which has led (or could lead) to litigation that may reach the court again.

    According to recent reports, the Democratic Party’s decisive victory in the midterm elections, which gave it a majority in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, could theoretically hinder Trump’s plans. However, Democrats would need not just a majority to pass legislation curbing the president’s authority but a veto-proof majority: 67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House, which could be more difficult to obtain.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    California Gov. Gavin Newsom looks on during a bill-signing event Aug. 21, 2025, in Sacramento, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

    District attorneys and victims’ families have taken their fight to the California Supreme Court over California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute over 500 death row penalty sentences.

    The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which represents the plaintiffs, argued Monday that the governor was required to give formal notice to district attorneys before commuting 548 death penalty sentences. The plaintiffs also challenged Newsom’s broad death penalty commutations without considering individual circumstances, beyond whether a person has more than one felony conviction. Existing law permits crime victims the opportunity to speak before a governor can commute someone.

    Recent findings suggest that “Gov. Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” the plaintiffs said. “He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

    In a recent development, newsom unveiled Nov. 5 the commutations of all people on death row to life in prison without parole. The governor wrote a letter that stated state-sanctioned killing undermines the legal system’s foundation and counters California’s values.

    Newsom, who has served two terms, declared a moratorium on all executions in 2019 and leaves office in January.

    Newsom moves to commute 548 death sentences, emptying California’s death row.
