    Tech Report: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • It has been revealed that this process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    It has been revealed that this process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    Sources indicate that this process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an key glitch of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an glitch that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    Recent findings suggest that the answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an crucial issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    In a recent development, the cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    And the justices rarely discuss it. In his upcoming book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    It has been revealed that many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    Industry observers note that caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    In a recent development, question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    The number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    It has been revealed that there are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    Industry observers note that these interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    Sources indicate that different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer newly introduced laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a company based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the matter (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    Industry observers note that question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal complications, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    It has been revealed that A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that the process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

    #43875. What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2420 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • Recent findings suggest that on Oct.
    • Sources indicate that in all of these cases, including this one, the policies at concern are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Recent findings suggest that on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in Newly introduced York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

    Sources indicate that in all of these cases, including this one, the policies at concern are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

    At glitch in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Initiative.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed a cut-off. Admission is then determined by a lottery from among those students who meet these requirements. Because schools in the region differ in their racial composition, basing admissions decisions on how well students score relative to other students in their same school ultimately affects the demographic composition of admitted students. AFEF claims that the Pandemic Plan violates equal protection because Montgomery County adopted it in order to change the racial demographics of the magnet schools and the plan had the effect of decreasing the share of Asian-American and white students.

    It has been revealed that according to the approach used by all of the courts evaluating magnet school admission practices, these facially neutral policies only violate equal protection if they are adopted for an impermissible reason (the intent element) and produce a discriminatory effect (the effect element). In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the district court found that the plaintiff had not alleged facts sufficient to satisfy either prong and so the school board’s motion to dismiss was granted. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit affirmed on the grounds that the district court properly evaluated whether there was a discriminatory effect.

    When and why facially neutral policies violate equal protection is a hotly contested glitch. Consider first the intent element. While all agree that the intention to exclude members of a particular racial group is invidious, there is disagreement about whether the intent to increase racial diversity is also impermissible. The Supreme Court has not yet directly ruled on this crucial issue and will not do so in this case. The cert grant in AFEF v. Montgomery County focuses only on the second element: the discriminatory effect. In particular, the Supreme Court limited its grant of AFEF’s petition to the following question: “Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”.

    This framing of the question roughly tracks the debate in the circuits between two different ways of showing discriminatory effect. In order to illustrate, let’s set aside the intent prong and assume it has been satisfied, either because the policy was actually adopted in order to reduce the percentage of Asian or white students in the magnet schools (though this fact is in dispute) or because the intention to increase the racial diversity of the schools is an impermissible intention (though this legal claim is contested). According to the 4th Circuit in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp. v. School Committee for the City of Boston, the effect element would be satisfied if a lower percentage of Asian or white students are admitted than applied. For example, if Asian students represent 30% of the applicant pool but only 20% of the admitted class, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. However, if 40% of the admitted class are Asian, then no discriminatory effect would be found because Asian students would in this case constitute a higher percentage of the admitted class than their 30% share in the applicant pool. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, both the district court and the 4th Circuit followed this approach.

    According to recent reports, by contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit in Sargent v. School District of Philadelphia, the dissenting judge in Coalition for TJ, and Justice Samuel Alito in his dissent from the denial of cert. in that case, assess discriminatory effect differently. Rather than compare the percentage of admitted students of the race alleged to be intentionally excluded to their percentage in the wider applicant pool, these jurists look to see if there has been a decrease in the percentage of admitted students of this race under the upcoming policy as compared to the prior policy. When a meaningful decrease is present, this constitutes a discriminatory effect. For example, if 50% of the admitted class were Asian under the prior policy and 40% are Asian under the new policy, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. And this would be so even if Asian students are still “overrepresented” in the sense that the percentage admitted is higher than their percentage of the applicant pool (30% in this example). In an article evaluating each of these approaches, we call this second approach the “Before-After Comparison” or “BAC,” and we call the first approach the “Population Comparison” or “PC.”.

    Yet both the PC and the BAC, as means of assessing discriminatory effect, have significant flaws. Let’s begin with the PC – the test used by the 4th and 1st Circuits. Recall that because the doctrine requires both impermissible intent and a discriminatory effect, it requires something more than just the fact that a policy is chosen for an invidious reason. The PC would effectively allow deliberate attempts to exclude Asians so long as they do well enough overall and do not fall below their share of the applicant pool. That seems problematic.

    Next consider the BAC, the test adopted by the 3rd Circuit, on which the discriminatory effect prong is satisfied only if the percentage of Asian students declines under the new policy. This test puts a strong thumb on the scale in favor of existing policies, whatever their merits, since sticking with the same policy is unlikely to result in major changes in the demographics of who is admitted. Thus a decision to keep things the same will evade scrutiny. And this is so even when maintaining a policy is done for uncontroversially bad reasons (say, because the existing policy is known to admit fewer Asian students, for example). In addition, the test is oversensitive to any changes in policy, since such changes are likely to lead to demographic shifts among the admitted students and thereby trigger a decrease for some group. While it is true that there will only be an equal protection violation if the school board at glitch intended this decrease, it remains the case that any change at all is risky because the effect element will likely always be satisfied for some group. For both these reasons, the BAC privileges the status quo and makes change difficult by making the status quo policy the normative baseline.

    The use of the term “aggregate” in the question on which certiorari was granted suggests that the court might think that the PC approach is flawed because it looks at how groups are treated rather than at how individuals are treated. And indeed it does. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the discriminatory effect element would be satisfied (using the PC) if the percentage of Asian and white students admitted was lower than the percentage of these groups among the fifth-grade students in the county. But the BAC is no different in this respect. It too looks at how a racial group fares under the Pandemic Plan. The BAC would find discriminatory effect if the percentage of Asian students admitted under the Pandemic Plan is less than the percentage admitted under the approach that preceded it. In other words, both tests for discriminatory effect focus on how the racial groups who are alleged to be the target of the invidious intentions fare as groups.

    Can either of these tests be reframed in ways that focus on how an individual is treated, rather than how members of her racial group are treated? After all, equal protection doctrine has long emphasized that the clause protects individuals rather than groups. Unfortunately, this is not easy to do. If a school uses race to decide which students to admit, it makes sense to say that a student’s race played a role in how she was treated. Facially neutral policies are different, however. Consider a simple and familiar facially neutral policy. Suppose a school board decides to admit the top 2% of each middle school to its coveted magnet high school. Suppose also that it does so, at least in part, to increase the racial diversity of the magnet school. Because there are more black and Latino students in some middle schools and more Asian and white students in others, this policy then produces a magnet school class that has a significant number of students of all races, let us suppose. Now consider an Asian student who is denied admissions because she is not in the top 2% of her middle school class. Has she been denied admission “because of her race?”.

    It has been revealed that one answer to this question could be simply “no.” Any student rejected by the admissions policy suffers a harm. It is this harm that gives the student standing to sue. But this rejection is not based on the student’s race when the school’s admissions policy is facially neutral. If this is correct (and if aggregate tests are out), then the court’s only option is to jettison the effect prong of the claim altogether. Were the court to take this route, facially neutral laws or policies would violate equal protection solely on the grounds that they were adopted with invidious intent.

    The U.S. Court of Appeal for the 2nd Circuit attempts a different approach. It uses the BAC to explain how individual students have suffered a discriminatory effect under a facially neutral policy. In Chinese American Citizens Alliance of Greater Latest York v. Adams, the percentage of Asian students admitted under the challenged admissions policy remained higher than their percentage in the applicant pool (thus failing to satisfy the PC in its aggregate form) and also did not decrease as compared to the prior admissions policy (thus failing to satisfy the BAC in its aggregate form). Yet the 2nd Circuit held that the effect element “can be satisfied by proof of an adverse harm to one or more individuals based on their race that has resulted from that discriminatory law or policy” (emphasis added). But the crucial question remains: in what way were the rejected Asian students rejected “because of their race” when race did not affect these decisions since the policy is facially neutral? The 2nd Circuit answers that question by referring to the fact that these students were “qualified for admission on an individual basis under the previous criteria" (emphasis added). In other words, in the view of the 2nd Circuit, if a new policy is adopted to exclude Asian students, then those Asian students who would have been admitted under the previous policy are denied admission because of their race.

    It has been revealed that this approach can be understood as an attempt to make the BAC individualized: the court here is determining whether a student’s rejection constitutes a distinctively discriminatory harm by drawing a comparison with how she would have fared under the previous policy. If this approach works (which we are agnostic about) for the BAC, a similar approach can be tailored for the PC as well. Here is how that would go. If a facially neutral policy was adopted in order to exclude Asian students and that policy is one under which Asian students are admitted at lower rates than students of other races, then each Asian student subject to that policy is subject to a policy that makes it harder for them to be admitted than it is for students of other races. On this view, each Asian student denied admission using this policy is then denied admission based on their race.

    In a recent development, thus, both tests can be articulated such that they capture a way that individual students are rejected based on their race. For this reason, the court should not choose one approach over the other on the grounds that one frames the injury in individual terms and the other looks at how groups are treated.

    This leaves the court with two options. First, as mentioned earlier, it could jettison the effect prong of the claim entirely and conclude that bad intentions alone render a facially neutral admissions policy impermissible. Doing so would put more pressure on the importance of answering the question of what intentions are invidious and, in particular, whether the intent to increase racial diversity is itself unconstitutional. Alternatively, the court must confront the question of discriminatory harm head-on and assess whether the BAC or PC provides the better account of it.

    It has been revealed that deborah Hellman is the Robert E. Scott Distinguished Professor of Law and the Honorable Albert V. Bryan Jr. ’50 Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, as well as Director of their Center for Law & Philosophy.

    Lily Hu is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at Yale University and also a contributing editor at Boston Review.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 17, 2026, 12:39 pm CST.

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology manufacturer Huawei, arguing that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Federal prosecutors urged jurors Monday to convict Chinese technology company Huawei, arguing during closing statements in the ongoing 11-week trial involving trade secrets theft and sanctions evasion that the company had grown by repeatedly committing crimes.

    In a recent development, according to a Monday story from Law.com, Meredith Arfa, the assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Latest York, told jurors that Huawei spent two decades pursuing growth “by any means possible.”.

    Recent findings suggest that to illustrate the trade secrets allegations, Arfa played a video of a former Huawei employee removing part of Tappy, T-Mobile’s robot for testing phone touchscreens, from the carrier’s lab. She also showed side-by-side images of Cisco’s and Huawei’s router source code, saying the two matched exactly—down to an engineer’s stray comment mentioning someone named “Bob.”.

    “This simply couldn’t happen without copying,” Arfa said in her summation.

    She further alleged that Huawei managers encouraged theft by paying bonuses for obtaining confidential competitor information, and that employees boasted about it on an internal forum.

    Sources indicate that on the sanctions compliance allegations, prosecutors remarked Huawei secretly controlled Skycom, a subsidiary that supplied sensitive technology to Iran’s government. Arfa said the firm repeatedly lied about owning Skycom. She also pointed to admissions by Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer, who signed a deferred prosecution agreement after spending three years under house arrest. Meng acknowledged that Skycom’s operations violated U.S. sanctions, and that she misled HSBC, Huawei’s primary bank, about its compliance, Arfa noted.

    Huawei, one of the largest telecommunications companies in the world, denies the allegations, contending that the case rests on the independent actions of rogue employees who were disciplined.

    The government announced the case in 2019. The company is represented by Jenner & Block, Sidley Austin and Steptoe.

    Breaking: The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session.
    • It has been revealed that today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review.
    • In a recent development, on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session. It also decided an interim docket case on border wall construction in southwestern Texas, granting the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to continue construction in an apparent 8-1 vote.

    It has been revealed that today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

    In a recent development, on Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew. Just over an hour later, Pavatt was executed in Oklahoma.

    It has been revealed that on Tuesday, the justices heard oral argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Industry observers note that on Monday, the justices heard argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Also on Monday, the justices heard argument in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

    Industry observers note that later on Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

    In Monday’s order list, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists.

    Sources indicate that in early October, a high school wrestler in Washington state and her mother came to the Supreme Court’s interim docket and asked the justices to prevent transgender girls from competing against her during this year’s wrestling season. The application has been fully briefed since Oct. 15, but the Supreme Court has not yet taken action. In a Monday letter, the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association asked the court not to intervene, highlighting the passage last week of a ballot initiative in Washington that aims to prevent “biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities that have separate classifications for male and female students” at K-12 schools.

    While speaking to the Federalist Society on Thursday, Justice Samuel Alito “warned against any potential congressional action to defund the Supreme Court as he defended the importance of an independent judiciary,” according to The Hill. “Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities,” he mentioned. “So, it is crucial to preserve the independence of the judiciary. If that is eliminated, then the Constitution as adopted in 1789 will no longer be the same.” He also described the judicial branch as “the least powerful branch,” adding that “it is ‘vulnerable’ to Congress and the executive.” But that doesn’t mean judges can’t go too far, Alito added. “If you think about a hand grenade, a 500-pound bomb and a nuclear weapon,” he said, “the hand grenade is the least dangerous. But that is not to say that it is not dangerous.”.

    According to recent reports, in February, “the Supreme Court struck down tariffs President Donald Trump imposed last year under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act,” holding that the law does not grant the president the power to impose tariffs. The next month, the U.S. Court of International Trade “ordered Customs and Border Patrol to matter refunds to importers totaling about $166 billion.” Now, seven Senate Democrats are asking the Federal Trade Commission “to investigate whether large corporations that received billions of dollars in tariff refunds violated federal law by not passing them on to their customers,” according to USA Today. “By increasing consumer prices, ostensibly due to tariff costs, and then refusing to provide refunds to consumers when they are later reimbursed for those tariff costs,” the senators wrote, “corporations may be in violation of the” Federal Trade Commission Act, which “empowers the commission to prevent ‘unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.’”.

    During a Thursday panel at the Federalist Society’s annual National Lawyers Convention, “White House counsel Will Scharf praised the Supreme Court’s June decision strengthening presidential firing power as a ‘generational win’” that “righted what he viewed as a ‘historic constitutional wrong,’” according to The Hill. “A president who can’t control who’s exercising the executive power that is vested in him, that’s a cabined presidency,” Scharf stated. “The Supreme Court did a masterful job,” he added. “Really got it right.”.

    On Thursday, former death row inmate Richard Glossip appeared in Oklahoma County District Court “for what was supposed to be his second hearing on pretrial motions” in the state’s effort to retry him for the 1997 murder of Barry Van Treese. “However, the hearing took a turn when the state announced an agreement between the prosecution and the defense,” under which “Glossip pleaded guilty to one count of accessory to murder,” according to KOKH in Oklahoma City. The plea agreement comes after the Supreme Court in 2025 “threw out Glossip’s murder conviction and death sentence,” determining that prosecutors had failed to correct false testimony. “Glossip’s sentencing is set for Dec. 17 and Dec. 18.”.

    Adam Liptak, The New York Times.

    Industry observers note that in his newsletter for The Upcoming York Times, Adam Liptak highlighted “hurdles and roadblocks [] erected by the Supreme Court” that may stand in the way of at least some of the new Congress’ planned investigations into “the Trump administration and its allies.” For example, in 2024’s Trump v. United States, in which the court granted the president “substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.” “Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding ‘which crimes to investigate and prosecute.’” It is also significant, according to Liptak, that “the court has never definitively resolved” whether Congress can “sue the executive branch,” an matter that will likely arise if the administration refuses “to give Congress documents or let officials testify.” Liptak noted that “it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate” disputes between Congress and the executive branch over access to information, “or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.”.

    During the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats in cases on birthright citizenship, tariffs, and his effort to fire Lisa Cook. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those complications.

    It has been revealed that in his Nuts and Bolts column, Stephen Wermiel explored how the Supreme Court decides what cases to decide, also known as the certiorari or “cert.” process. According to him, “questions will continue to arise about how th[is] process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.”.

    Industry observers note that in a column for SCOTUSblog, Deborah Hellman and Lily Hu revisited the Supreme Court’s decision to grant review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on the circumstances under which facially neutral admissions policies violate equal protection by producing a discriminatory effect.

    In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored 11 petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices during today’s conference, which cover such problems as the Trump administration’s effort to remove certain noncitizens from the country without first allowing them to apply for asylum and a ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”.

    In his Born Free and Equal column on Wednesday, Steven Calabresi reviewed Justice Samuel Alito’s latest book and commended it as “exceptionally intellectual and provocative.” “The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not,” Calabresi concluded.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Amy reported that the Trump administration has once again asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to build a newly introduced White House ballroom. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in her inaugural Substance and Procedure column on Monday, Rachel Bayefsky explored the Supreme Court’s application of a “history-and-tradition” analysis in recent cases on the constitutionality of agency adjudication – that is, “the practice of resolving disputes ‘in-house’ within administrative agencies instead of addressing” them in a court. According to Bayefsky, the court’s decision in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards “may have an notable impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.”.

    In a recent development, sarah Isgur and David French analyze free speech problems from the past three election cycles, including Donald Trump’s “they/them” ad in 2024 and the Trump administration’s threats to social media companies. They then discuss a free speech fight that may define the next two years.

    The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Samuel Nelson, who served on the court from 1845 to 1872.

    According to recent reports, while you might think there’s only one justice with the name Samuel based on recent news coverage, there have actually been five with that first name in the court’s history – and in today’s justice biography, we’ll take a look at the second. (The first, if you recall, didn’t get things off to a particularly great start: He is the only justice to have been impeached.).

    Although referred to as “one of those nineteenth-century justices of whom we often lose sight” (the Journal of Supreme Court History said it, not us), Justice Samuel Nelson served on the court for 27 years as a “pragmatic yet low-key man,” as described by Oyez. Things began for him in Hebron, New York, where he was born in November 1792 to Scot-Irish farmers. His father helped pay Nelson’s Middlebury College tuition by selling a person who was enslaved. Nelson graduated from Middlebury in 1813; clerked at a Salem law firm; followed one of its partners to Madison County, New York when the firm split; and was admitted to the bar in 1817 (two years later, he married his law firm practice partner’s daughter).

    In 1820, Nelson was appointed the town’s postmaster and served as a presidential elector for James Monroe. He became a delegate to the 1821 state constitutional convention, where he pushed to eliminate property requirements for male voters.

    Fresh York Gov. Joseph Yates appointed Nelson as a state circuit judge in 1823. Gov. Enos Throop elevated him to the New York Supreme Court of Judicature (that state’s highest trial court) in 1831, and he became its chief justice in 1837. In Jack v. Martin, he held that New York could not interfere with enforcement of the federal Fugitive Slave Act and noted that anyone who seized a free man would, under state law, “be answerable like any other trespasser or kidnapper.”.

    Industry observers note that in 1845, Nelson ran for the U.S. Senate and lost. Shortly after, President John Tyler nominated him to succeed Justice Smith Thompson. The Senate confirmed Nelson by voice vote in February 1845, and he served as circuit justice for the 2nd Circuit (Connecticut, New York, and Vermont) while on the Supreme Court.

    According to recent reports, on the bench, Nelson “kept a low profile,” generally voting with the majority. He did write a few notable decisions, one of them in 1850’s Hotchkiss v. Greenwood, a landmark patent law case. In 1857’s Fellows v. Blacksmith, Nelson wrote for a unanimous court that a land manufacturer could not forcibly evict the Tonawanda Senecas, calling such litigation “appalling.” According to one scholar, Nelson “persuaded all his brethren, including those who had supported Jacksonian Indian removal policies, of the merits of the Tonawandas’ Seneca treaty arguments.” The same scholar wrote that Fellows eventually allowed for the treaty that let the tribe buy back 7,500 acres of its reservation.

    In a recent development, fellows was decidedthe same year as Dred Scott v. Sandford. Nelson reportedly resisted behind-the-scenes pressure from incoming President James Buchanan to endorse at least part of Chief Justice Roger Taney’s opinion (unlike Justice Robert Grier). Nevertheless, he concurred with the majority, and scholars have “castigat[ed] him, along with Justice Robert Grier of Pennsylvania, for being the only two Northern jurists on the bench who voted with the majority in the case.” (Ten years later in Georgia v. Stanton, Nelson refused to let Georgia block Congress’ Reconstruction program, holding that its claims “call for the judgment of the court upon political questions.”).

    Sources indicate that in the lead-up to the Civil War, Nelson and Justice John Campbell acted as intermediaries between Secretary of State William Seward and Southern commissioners who wanted the Confederacy recognized. Privately, Nelson wrote on Christmas Day in 1860 that “we almost despair of the republic” and in 1862 wrote to Justice Benjamin Curtis that he hoped the country might survive both “the fierceness of the enemy without and imbecility of the authorities within.”.

    It has been revealed that nelson also dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not legally blockade Southern ports until Congress declared war. The dissent (along with his vote in Ex parte Milligan to overturn the conviction of a man charged with helping the Confederacy and opposing expanding federal power) led critics to question his loyalty to the Union.

    Following the civil war, President Ulysses S. Grant in 1871 named the 79-year-old Nelson one of five American members of the commission handling claims against Great Britain for the damages caused by British-built Confederate ships, which Nelson accepted (although he wrote that he was “hardly at liberty to refuse”). The proceedings won the United States $15.5 million.

    Nelson retired in November 1872. He died in Cooperstown, Upcoming York, in December 1873, at age 81. One historian wrote that Nelson was a “quietly competent jurist” in comparison to several of “his more flamboyant and controversial judicial brethren” (some of whom we will be covering soon).

    On Nov. 10, Judge Richard Posner passed away at the age of 87. Posner, who served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit from 1981 to 2017, was one of the most influential jurists never to have served on the Supreme Court. In addition to his voluminous opinions (some affirmed, others denied), Posner authored over 60 books and more than 500 articles and served as a Senior Lecturer in Law at the University of Chicago Law School. Among his many contributions, Posner helped give life to the law and economics movement and to the study of judging as an empirical pursuit. As Zach, our executive editor, can attest to first-hand, he was both charming and hilarious in person and did not suffer bad ideas lightly. But this is SCOTUSblog. So what did Posner have to say about the court specifically? Here are some choice quotations (you may notice a theme):.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The prediction market unsuccessfully argued federal law preempts the state from requiring it to comply with state laws on problems like deceptive advertising.Â.
    • (CN) â A Fourth Circuit majority joined two other federal appellate courts Wednesday in holding that prediction markets like Kalshi are subject to state gambling laws.
    • Recent findings suggest that “Congress knows how to displace traditional state police powers when it chooses to do so,” U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The prediction market unsuccessfully argued federal law preempts the state from requiring it to comply with state laws on problems like deceptive advertising.Â.

    RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â A Fourth Circuit majority joined two other federal appellate courts Wednesday in holding that prediction markets like Kalshi are subject to state gambling laws.

    Recent findings suggest that “Congress knows how to displace traditional state police powers when it chooses to do so,” U.S. Circuit Judge Roger Gregory, a George W. Bush appointee, mentioned. “Here, it has not done so with the clarity our precedents require.”.

    In a recent development, A Maryland federal judge denied Kalshi injunctive relief that would have blocked Maryland from requiring it to obtain a license to offer sports betting. Kalshi argued the Commodity Exchange Act gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission exclusive jurisdiction over swaps â a type of derivative contract dependent on the occurrence of an event associated with a potential financial consequence.

    In a recent development, “When betting platforms operate outside state oversight, Marylanders lose the protections that keep gambling fair and safe,” Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown said in a statement. “Today’s ruling means Kalshi must meet the same consumer protection standards as every other sportsbook serving Maryland residents.”.

    Industry observers note that writing for the majority, Gregory ruled that the lower court properly framed the preemption question not as whether the sports event contracts offered are swaps, but whether Congress intended to preempt the state’s historic police power to regulate gambling. Gregory concluded Congress did not clearly and manifestly intend to preempt state gambling laws.

    Recent findings suggest that “The question is therefore not whether Congress regulates these contracts through the CEA,” the George W. Bush appointee mentioned. “Rather, the question is whether Congress clearly intended the CEA to vest the CFTC with exclusive regulatory authority over gaming contracts, thereby withdrawing Maryland’s historic authority to regulate gambling in this area.”.

    According to recent reports, U.S. Circuit Judge Stephanie Thacker joined Gregory’s opinion, differing however by arguing the preemption question turns on whether the sports event contracts are swaps. Thacker, agreeing with Gregory’s ultimate ruling, argued the sports contracts are not swaps subject to the commission’s exclusive regulatory authority.

    Recent findings suggest that “I reject the idea that the outcome of a sporting event is itself an event,” the Barack Obama appointee noted in a concurring opinion. “Instead, I would adopt the common sense conclusion that an event, in the sports context, is the contest or match itself.”.

    Recent findings suggest that gregory pointed to Congress’s passage of the Dodd-Frank Act, which prevents the commission from allowing trading of unlawful events, including assassinations or terrorist attacks. The Dodd-Frank Act also lists trading on “gaming” as against the public interest and thus not authorized through the Commodity Exchange Act. According to Gregory, the Dodd-Frank Act reveals that preemption is not resolved by whether event contracts are swaps.

    Gregory disagreed with Kalshi’s argument that the commission’s federal authority over exchange trading displaces state laws addressing the separate states’ interests that Congress directed the commission to consider under the Dodd-Frank Act. Gregory also disagreed with Kalshi that state laws conflict with the Commodities Exchange Act.

    “It does not determine whether a gaming contract may be listed or traded on a DCM â that authority remains with the CFTC,” Gregory said of Maryland’s gambling law. “Instead, it imposes generally applicable conditions on entities that choose to offer these sports event contracts within Maryland, including obligations to obtain a license and comply with applicable advertising restrictions.”.

    U.S. Circuit Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin dissented from the majority. The Joe Biden appointee ruled the contracts are swaps.

    In a recent development, “The dissent’s view would allow Kalshi, or any person or entity for that matter, to circumvent state gambling laws by repackaging ordinary gambling as futures trading on a DCM,” Gregory noted. “The statutory context of the CEA does not evince a ‘clear and manifest’ intention to preempt traditional state authority and permit this loophole.”.

    Industry observers note that the Fourth Circuit joined the Sixth and Ninth Circuits in ruling that states can regulate Kalshi. A divided Third Circuit panel determined the Commodity Exchange Act prevents Fresh Jersey sports betting laws from regulating Kalshi’s sports event contracts.Â Many experts believe the Supreme Court will have to step in to resolve the circuit split.

    Sources indicate that “Judges can’t agree with each other on why we’re wrong,” Kalshi spokesperson Elizabeth Diana stated. “This splintered decision, including three separate contradictory opinions, demonstrates there is no unified coherent legal argument against prediction markets.”.

    #43869. Breaking: Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1119 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Tribal property and the Supreme Court

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that one of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights.
    • It has been revealed that before the court is a petition to review the U.S.
    • Though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that one of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock), Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “atmosphere” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

    It has been revealed that before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline tech giant. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

    Though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in Oneida County v. Oneida Indian Nation, which held that there is a federal common law cause of action allowing Indigenous property owners to bring trespass actions in federal court.

    The Andeavor case has been accompanied in recent years by a slate of lower court decisions similarly diminishing Indigenous property rights. In Davilla v. Enable Midstream Partners, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit held that a pipeline trespasser on Indigenous property would not be ordered to remove the pipeline until the federal district court decided it was, among other things, in the “public interest” to do so. Under federal law, federal courts may not order injunctive relief unless such relief is in the public interest. The 10th Circuit’s decision imposed a public interest standard on Indigenous property when, arguably, it would not have done so in relation to private property.

    It has been revealed that similarly, a judge on the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin held in Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe Indians v. Enbridge Inc. that the tribe was not entitled to the immediate removal of a trespassing pipeline because the public interest favored its continued operation. Fortunately, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit reversed that decision. Other federal courts have also ordered immediate eviction of trespassers to Indigenous lands (e.g., United States v. Osage Wind), but the judiciary tends to invoke the public interest when favoring pipeline or other petroleum industry companies.

    Industry observers note that newland argues that some judges may be channeling a long tradition where the federal government assumed that Indigenous property is public property: Most pipelines running through Indigenous lands now originated in an earlier era where the federal government assumed a kind of guardianship over tribal nations, where the Interior Department granted easements and rights-of-way over Indigenous lands without tribal consent. For example, the Supreme Court once held that the secretary of the Interior was empowered to problem leases to natural resources extraction companies even over tribal opposition (Cherokee Nation v. Hitchcock).

    The tradition of guardianship arose in early Supreme Court decisions comparing the federal-tribal relationship to a “guardian-ward” relationship (Cherokee Nation v. Georgia). Congress did not enact laws generally asserting actual guardianship over tribal nations; instead, the relationship was more accurately characterized as a trust relationship, with federal government owning and managing tribal and individual Indian asserts in trust.

    A trust beneficiary has legal rights that a ward does not. A ward does not possess the legal capacity to make their own decisions, while tribal nations and tribal citizens do. When federal or state actors did assert guardianship over Indigenous assets, tragedy often followed, as evidenced in the early 20th century killings of Osage people fictionalized in the film “Killers of the Flower Moon” or in the flooding of several Indian reservations in the mid-20th century by federal hydroelectric dam projects.

    Often, when tribal nations attempted to assert their own legal rights, the judiciary allowed the federal government to block those efforts. Justice Neil Gorsuch recently raised this problem in his dissent in Arizona v. Navajo Nation, where he pointed out that, decades ago, the federal government blocked the Navajo Nation from asserting their water rights, which remain unsettled to this day. In those older cases, the fact that the federal government could stand in the shoes of Indigenous interests suggested that Indigenous property was therefore, in effect, public property.

    Recent findings suggest that the Department of Justice’s litigation positions also frequently hearken back to expansive federal controls over Indigenous property. While the Supreme Court has explicitly overturned the earlier cases analogizing the federal-tribal relationship as a guardianship in cases such as United States v. Sioux Nation, DOJ attorneys are known to continue to assert guardianship-type control over Indigenous property. Indeed, federal judges have sanctioned them for making such claims post-Sioux Nation.

    This legacy of guardianship once again has raised its head. D.C. Circuit briefing has concluded in a claim brought by the Tohono O’Odham Nation against the Department of Homeland Security regarding the administration’s plan to build a border wall on the tribe’s land. The tribe argues that the federal common law cause of action recognized in Oneida undergirds the suit. In response, the DOJ now asserts that tribal nations may not sue the United States for trespass on hands held in trust by the federal government for the benefit of a tribal nation. This claim rings again of guardianship, where a ward normally does not have the legal capacity to sue their guardian.

    The import of the government’s claim in the border wall case, like the trespass action in Andeavor, has enormous consequences for Indian country: If the government can confiscate Indigenous property held in trust by the United States, then the judiciary will have allowed the federal government to reassume a guardianship-type relationship regardless of tribal consent or the federal government’s trust duties.

    In a recent development, matthew L.M. Fletcher is the Harry Burns Hutchins Collegiate Professor of Law at the University of Michigan Law School.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

    According to recent reports, the AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. Traffic from AI clients and agents behaves differently from traffic from people: hundreds of calls a minute, retry loops, and no reading of deprecation warnings. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

    Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

    In a recent development, define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

    In a recent development, participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

    Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring concerns into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

    Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

    Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

    Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

    Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

    Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

    Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

    Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

    Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

    Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

    Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

    Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

    Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

    Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

    Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving swiftly.

    Industry observers note that pick your centre of gravity. We expect you to be deep in at least one of these, and to tell us which:.

    APIs and auth: You have designed permission models, token scopes or OAuth flows for third-party or machine clients, and you have migrated them without breaking users.

    Operations: You have run production services yourself: carried the pager, written alerts and runbooks, used SLOs or similar to decide what to fix, and made shared systems less risky over time.

    Gateways and distributed systems: You have built or run proxies or gateways, or debugged hard failures across services (retries, partial failures, upstream outages, fail-open vs fail-closed decisions), and you can reason about load and degradation.

    Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

    Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

    Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

    Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

    In a recent development, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    It has been revealed that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    Sources indicate that once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

    According to recent reports, in a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, James remarked he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

    There is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants introduced a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

    It has been revealed that “The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he currently wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

    “Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”.

    The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

    Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

    A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

    WASHINGTON (CN) â The Trump administration called on the Supreme Court Wednesday to intervene for a third time in the ongoing fight over protected status for Venezuelan migrants living in the U.S.

    In an emergency application, the Department of Homeland Security warned that a looming lower court decision could force the government to resurrect temporary protected status â known as TPS â for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants after a 19-month hiatus.

But the administration says the appeals courtâs subpar response threatened to reinstate a decision allowing Venezuelan migrants to regain access to the program within days.

    âGiving effect to the district courtâs order for even a moment at this late date will gravely harm the government, compelling it to release removable aliens into the country with no guarantee of ever successfully locating them and returning them to detention,â U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer wrote. âIt will also cause mass confusion by requiring work authorizations for thousands of aliens to flip on and off as litigation progresses.â.

    Temporary Protected Status is a designation applied to nationals of certain countries where violence or economic duress makes deportation difficult or unsafe. Venezuelans make up the largest number of such status holders in the nation.

    In a recent development, before leaving office, former President Joe Biden issued an 18-month TPS extension for Venezuelans. In February 2025, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem revoked the extension, ending TPS status for almost 350,000 migrants.

    Industry observers note that during a Fox News interview, Noem called Venezuelan immigrants âdirtbagsâ and insinuated they were members of criminal gangs. Venezuelan migrants and the National TPS Alliance, an immigrant advocacy group, sued the administration, claiming that Noemâs actions were unlawful and motivated by racial animus.

    After reviewing the case for a second time, a lower court again blocked the administrationâs revocation, leading to a follow-up emergency appeal at the Supreme Court. In October 2025, the court reversed once more, leading to a dissent from the three Democratic appointees.

    That decision remained in place while the justices reviewed a similar TPS revocation challenge from Syrian and Haitian migrants earlier this year. In June, the conservative majority ruled to block courts from reviewing the administrationâs decisions on TPS designations.

    The Ninth Circuit was instructed to review Venezuelan migrantsâ case under the upcoming precedent. But the government mentioned the appeals court has yet to issue an updated stay to prevent the lower court ruling from going back into effect.

    The White House urged the justices to step in for a third time, calling the Ninth Circuitâs refusal to grant a stay inexplicable.

    âThis court already balanced these very equities twice before and found that they tilted in the governmentâs favor; that should be dispositive this third time,â Sauer wrote.

    According to the solicitor general, the government would be forced to immediately release 1,800 Venezuelan migrants from detention without a ruling by Friday. The government would also be prevented from executing over 300 removal orders and be forced to glitch work authorizations.

    The Supreme Court did not immediately respond to the application.

    • Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    As the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it. There are important disputes tied to climate change, immigration, and the Second Amendment. But no case is quite comparable to last term’s battles over tariffs, birthright citizenship, executive authority, and the Voting Rights Act.

    Just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases. Perhaps of even greater note, though, is that it’s short on cases in general, as the court is running behind its typical pace for grants.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    It has been revealed that “You would have paid a yearly fee, and that’s presumably to use it 365 days a year. And so, if you didn’t have the ability to use it, there’s a certain amount of money that was collected where services were not offered,” said attorney Jeff Orenstein of Consumer Law Group in a Wednesday interview.

    Dinelle also claims Microsoft should have anticipated the outage â given two other major outages in 2025 â and made efforts to prevent the issue.

    “Defendants committed faults in failing to prevent the service interruption to the Microsoft 365 services in light of previous recent service interruptions to Microsoft 365,” she writes in the suit filed Monday.

    Industry observers note that according to Microsoft in a report released Monday, the source of the outage was a combination of a latent defect from July and a reduced server capacity overwhelmed its systems. The American tech giant assured the public the blackout was not the result of a cyberattack.

    According to recent reports, in the class action made available Wednesday, Dinelle is seeking to represent affected individual consumers in Canada. Orenstein explained that businesses that use those platforms are not included in the proceedings because they have arbitration clauses that do not apply to individual users in Quebec.

    But in another class action filed Monday and made available Tuesday, Metus Lykos Debt Law looks to represent all Canadians, including businesses, affected by the outage.

    “A 24-hour email blackout isn’t a minor inconvenience when your business runs on it. There are lost customers, missed deadlines and employees you still have to pay,” said attorney Darryl Singer of Diamond & Diamond Lawyers representing the law firm. “Microsoft sold reliability. This lawsuit asks who pays when that reliability fails.”.

    It has been revealed that both class actions name the Washington state-based Microsoft Corporation and Toronto-based Microsoft Canada Inc. as defendants.

    In the lawsuit filed in Ontario Superior Court, Metus Lykos claims Microsoft was negligent and breached the contract it held with its owners by failing to prevent the outage.

    “Before the outage, the defendants represented that the affected services were reliable and highly available, and that they had designed and operated them to prevent and contain outages,” the law firm claims in the suit.

    Diamond & Diamond estimated economic losses from business disruption, lost productivity and other expenses could amount up to CA$100 million, or $67 million.

    Courthouse News reporter Tatiana Mulowayi-Pelletier is based in Montreal, Canada.
